newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico sees 1996 GDP growth at 3.7 pct - Ortiz.
newsitem.headline: Mexico sees 1996 GDP growth at 3.7 pct - Ortiz.

text.p: Mexican Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz predicted that 1996 gross domestic product (GDP) growth would end the year at about 3.7 percent.

In a statement giving a broad outline of 1997 budget proposals to the Mexican Congress, Ortiz said the government estimated that GDP growth in 1997 would be "at least 4.0 percent, based on export growth, stepped-up public and private investment and a gradual recovery of consumption."
Ortiz said 1997 inflation would be 15 percent, following inflation in 1996 that is expected to end the year "at about half the 52 percent registered in 1995."
He reiterated the government would run a slight budget deficit of 0.5 percent of GDP, due mostly to the cost of pension reforms and the bank bailout program.
"Notwithstanding these costs, by making more efficient use of funds, and under the current tax regime, investment and public savings will increase significantly," he said.
Ortiz estimated that the 1997 current account deficit would be about 1.2 percent of GDP.
He said the 4 growth target for 1997 was "an achievable target" due to a favorable outlook for investment and other components of aggregate demand.
He said total public investment would equal 4 percent of GDP, focused mostly on infrastructure projects in the oil, electricity, highway, water and housing sectors.
Ortiz said the investment in the export sector and the projected economic growth in Mexico's main trading partners should allow Mexican exports to fuel a recovery.
He also said a "gradual recovery" in real wages next year will allow "a moderate" recovery of consumption.

Ortiz said Mexico will stick by its current regime of a free floating peso during next year. He said the regime was the best one for an open economy and is necessary to spur a competitive export sector.
